analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug payments at the lower of VA or federal supply prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote; it was referred to the Finance Committee on May 4, 2023 and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force drug makers to sell Medicare-covered drugs at no more than the lower of two government purchase prices: what the Department of Veterans Affairs pays, or what the General Services Administration pays through its federal supply schedule. Because the government already negotiates steep discounts through those channels, Medicare payments for drugs under Parts B and D would drop sharply, and the government says that would roughly cut Medicare drug prices in half. Drug companies that refused to accept the price would lose Medicare coverage for their drugs entirely. The bill was introduced by Senator Bernie Sanders and never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would pay less out of pocket for prescription drugs, and taxpayers, who fund a large share of Medicare drug spending and would bear less of the cost of prices above the government-purchase cap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps Medicare payment for every covered Part B and Part D drug at the lower of the price the Department of Veterans Affairs pays or the price on the General Services Administration's federal supply schedule, both of which are steeply negotiated government prices.
To keep Medicare coverage for a drug, a manufacturer must agree to supply it at or below that capped amount, so companies could not simply opt out and keep charging Medicare more.
The cap would apply to drugs furnished or dispensed on or after January 1, 2024, overriding the usual Part B payment formula and the Part D negotiated-price rules.

Because Medicare covers tens of millions of older and disabled Americans, a payment cap at government-purchase prices would mean lower drug costs for beneficiaries and lower federal spending on the same drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose Medicare revenue per drug would be cut to government-purchase price levels, with the cost of that reduction falling on their shareholders and on prices they charge elsewhere to make up the difference.

drawbacks.text: Pegging all Medicare prices to the VA's purchase prices could reduce drug company revenue below what it takes to develop some new medicines, which drug makers and some economists argue would mean fewer new drugs over time.

The bill sets prices by reference to two existing government purchasing programs without any process for adjusting for cases where the VA or GSA price is unusually low or a drug is supplied under special terms, leaving the mechanics to later implementation.

Manufacturers facing a mandatory price floor at government rates would have an incentive to raise prices in non-Medicare channels, so some of the savings could be shifted to privately insured patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers would pay dramatically less for the same drugs, since the cap is tied to prices the government already successfully negotiates. The cost falls on an industry with some of the highest profit margins in the economy, and the main honest objection is the risk of somewhat less pharmaceutical research investment over time. How much innovation would actually be lost is disputed, and the bill contains no mechanism to tailor prices, but the core tradeoff favors the paying public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 4, 2023, with Senator Amy Klobuchar as its one cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles Medicare legislation.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers benefited, since a cap tying Medicare prices to government-purchase rates died in committee without a vote, leaving Medicare drug payments and their revenues untouched by this bill.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted it to the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 4, 2023 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose Medicare prices the bill would cap
against.what_they_did: Would have lost Medicare revenue under the bill; no recorded committee action advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split on the bill itself was never tested; its only support was one independent sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no Republicans signed on.

industries.note: The bill caps what Medicare pays for their drugs at the lower of the VA or federal supply schedule price and requires them to accept that price to keep Medicare coverage at all, cutting revenue on a large share of their U.S. sales. Their gain from the bill dying is the public's continued higher drug costs.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D prescription drug plans
industries.note: Part D plans and their intermediaries negotiate prices today and keep a spread between what they pay and what Medicare reimburses; a hard statutory price cap would compress that margin. Consumers would benefit from lower prices, but the middlemen's role would be squeezed rather than removed.

industries.industry: Community pharmacies and health providers billing Part B drugs
industries.note: Providers and pharmacies would be reimbursed at the lower capped prices, reducing revenue per drug, but their patients would face lower drug costs, which supports adherence and volume. The net effect depends on whether lower prices increase use enough to offset the per-unit cut.
